entries.eca12702d2ef542ca6651ec0afc0e2bff384a926: <div sID="gen15241" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Song.3" sID="Song.3"/> <div eID="gen15241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15242" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15243" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. The church gives an account of a sore trial wherewith she was exercised through the withdrawing of her beloved from her, the pains she was at before she recovered the comfortable sense of his favour again, and the resolution she took, when she did recover it, not to lose it again, as she had done through her own carelessness, <reference osisRef="Song.3.1-Song.3.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. The daughters of Jerusalem admire the excellencies of the church, <reference osisRef="Song.3.6">ver. 6</reference>. III. The church admires Jesus Christ under the person of Solomon, his bed, and the life-guards about it (<reference osisRef="Song.3.7-Song.3.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>), his chariot, <reference osisRef="Song.3.9-Song.3.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. She calls upon the daughters of Zion, who were admiring her, to admire him rather, especially as he appeared on his coronation day and the day of his nuptials, <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">ver. 11</reference>.
entries.983396fb27985d963ca882b61859b2fa06461401: <div eID="gen15243" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15242" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15244" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not. <hi type="super">2</hi> I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not. <hi type="super">3</hi> The watchmen that go about the city found me: <hi type="italic">to whom I said,</hi> Saw ye him whom my soul loveth? <hi type="super">4</hi> <hi type="italic">It was</hi> but a little that I passed from them, but I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me. <hi type="super">5</hi> I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake <hi type="italic">my</hi> love, till he please. <div eID="gen15244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15245" type="x-p"/> God is not wont to say to the seed of Jacob, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain;</hi> and yet here we have the spouse for a great while seeking her beloved in vain, but finding him at last, to her unspeakable satisfaction. It was hard to the Old-Testament church to find Christ in the ceremonial law, and the types and figures which then were <hi type="italic">of good things to come.</hi> Long was the consolation of Israel looked for before it came. The watchman of that church gave little assistance to those who enquired after him; but at length Simeon had <hi type="italic">him</hi> in his arms <hi type="italic">whom his soul loved.</hi> It is applicable to the case of particular believers, who often walk in darkness a great while, but <hi type="italic">at even time it shall be light,</hi> and those that seek Christ to the end shall find him at length. Observe, <div eID="gen15245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15246" type="x-p"/> I. How the spouse sought him in vain <hi type="italic">upon her bed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.3.1">v. 1</reference>); when she was up and looking about her, grace in act and exercise, though her beloved was withdrawn, yet she could see him at a distance (<reference osisRef="Song.2.8">ch. ii. 8</reference>), but now it was otherwise. She still continued her affection to him, still it was <hi type="italic">he whom her soul loved,</hi> that bond of the covenant still continued firm. "<hi type="italic">Though he slay me, I will trust in him;</hi> though he leave me, I will love him. When I have him not in my arms, I have him in my heart." But she wanted the communion she used to have with him, as David when he <hi type="italic">thirsted for God, for the living God.</hi> She sought him, but, 1. It was <hi type="italic">by night on her bed;</hi> it was late and lazy seeking. Her understanding was clouded; it was by night, in the dark. Her affections were chilled, it was on her bed half asleep. The wise virgins slumbered in the absence of the bridegroom. It was a dark time with the believer; she saw not her signs, and yet she sought them. Those whose souls love Jesus Christ will continue to seek him even in silence and solitude: their <hi type="italic">reins</hi> instruct them to do so, even <hi type="italic">in the night season.</hi> 2. She failed in her endeavour. Sometimes he is <hi type="italic">found of those that seek him not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">Isa. lxv. 1</reference>), but here he is not found of one that sought him, either for punishment of her corruptions, her slothfulness and security (we miss of comfort because we do not seek it aright), or for the exercises of grace, her faith and patience, to try whether she will continue seeking. The woman of Canaan sought Christ, and found him not at first, that she might find him, at length, so much the more to her honour and comfort. <div eID="gen15246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15247" type="x-p"/> II. How she had sought him in vain abroad, <reference osisRef="Song.3.2">v. 2</reference>. She had made trial of secret worship, and had gone through the duties of the closet, had remembered him on her bed and meditated on him in the <hi type="italic">night-watches</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.6">Ps. lxiii. 6</reference>), but she did not meet with comfort. <hi type="italic">My sore ran in the night,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">I remembered God and was troubled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.77.2-Ps.77.3">Ps. lxxvii. 2, 3</reference>. And yet she is not driven off by the disappointment from the use of further means; she resolves, "<hi type="italic">I will rise now;</hi> I will not lie here if I cannot find my beloved here, nor be content if he be withdrawn. <hi type="italic">I will rise now</hi> without delay, and seek him immediately, lest he withdraw further from me." Those that would seek Christ so as to find him must lose no time. "<hi type="italic">I will rise</hi> out of a warm bed, and go out in a cold dark night, in quest of my beloved." Those that see Christ must not startle at difficulties. "<hi type="italic">I will rise, and go about the city,</hi> the holy city, in the streets, and the broad-ways;" for she knew he was not to be found in any blind by-ways. We must seek in the city, in Jerusalem, which was a type of the gospel-church. The likeliest place to find Christ is in the temple (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.46">Luke ii. 46</reference>), in the streets of the gospel-church, in holy ordinances, where the children of Zion pass and repass at all hours. She had a good purpose when she said, <hi type="italic">I will arise now,</hi> but the good performance was all in all. She arose, and <hi type="italic">sought him</hi> (those that are in pursuit of Christ, the knowledge of him and communion with him, must turn every stone, seek every where), and yet she <hi type="italic">found him not;</hi> she was still unsatisfied, uneasy, as Job, when he looked on all sides, but could not perceive any tokens of the divine favour (<reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.9">Job xxiii. 8, 9</reference>), and the Psalmist often, when he complained that God hid his face from him, <reference osisRef="Ps.88.14">Ps. lxxxviii. 14</reference>. We may be in the way of our duty and yet may miss the comfort, for <hi type="italic">the wind bloweth where it listeth.</hi> How heavy is the accent on this repeated complaint: <hi type="italic">I sought him, but I found him not!</hi> like that of Mary Magdalen, <hi type="italic">They have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.20.13">John xx. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen15247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15248" type="x-p"/> III. How she enquired of the watchmen concerning him, <reference osisRef="Song.3.3">v. 3</reference>. In the night the watchmen <hi type="italic">go about the city,</hi> for the preservation of its peace and safety, to guide and assist the honest and quiet, as well as to be a check upon those that are disorderly; these met her in her walks, and she asked them if they could give her any tidings of her beloved. In the streets and broad-ways of Jerusalem she might meet with enough to divert her from her pursuit and to entertain her, though she could not meet her beloved; but she regards none in comparison with him. Gracious souls press through crowds of other delights and contentments in pursuit of Christ, whom they prefer before their chief joy. Mary Magdalen sees angels in the sepulchre, but that will not do unless she see Jesus. <hi type="italic">Saw you him whom my soul loveth?</hi> Note, We must evince the sincerity of our love to Christ by our solicitous enquiries after him. <hi type="italic">The children of the bride-chamber will mourn when the bridegroom is taken away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.15">Matt. ix. 15</reference>), especially for the sin which provoked him to withdraw; and, if we do so, we shall be in care to recover the sense of his favour and diligent and constant in the use of proper means in order thereunto. We must search the scriptures, be much in prayer, keep close to ordinances, and all with this upon our heart, <hi type="italic">Saw you him whom my soul loveth?</hi> Those only who have seen Christ themselves are likely to direct others to a sight of him. When the Greeks came to worship at the feast they applied to Philip, with such an address as this of the spouse to the watchmen, <hi type="italic">Sir, we would see Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.21">John xii. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen15248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15249" type="x-p"/> IV. How she found him at last, <reference osisRef="Song.3.4">v. 4</reference>. She <hi type="italic">passed from</hi> the watchmen as soon as she perceived they could give her no tidings of her beloved; she would not stay with them, because he was not among them, but went on seeking, for (as Ainsworth observes) the society neither of brethren, nor of the church, nor of ministers, can comfort the afflicted conscience unless Christ himself be apprehended by faith. But soon after she parted from the watchmen she found him whom she sought, and then called him <hi type="italic">him whom my soul loveth,</hi> with as much delight as before with desire. Note, Those that continue seeking Christ shall find him at last, and when perhaps they were almost ready to despair of finding him. See <reference osisRef="Ps.42.7-Ps.42.8">Ps. xlii. 7, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.9-Ps.77.10">lxxvii. 9, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.7-Isa.54.8">Isa. liv. 7, 8</reference>. Disappointments must not drive us away from gracious pursuits. Hold out, faith and patience; <hi type="italic">the vision is for an appointed time,</hi> and, though the watchman can give us no account of it, <hi type="italic">at the end</hi> it shall itself <hi type="italic">speak and not lie;</hi> and the comfort that comes in after long waiting, in the use of means, will be so much the sweeter at last. <div eID="gen15249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15250" type="x-p"/> V. How close she kept to him when she had found him. She is now as much in fear of losing him as before she was in care to find him: <hi type="italic">I held him,</hi> held him fast, as the women, when they met with Christ after his resurrection, <hi type="italic">held him by the feet, and worshipped him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.28.9">Matt. xxviii. 9</reference>. "<hi type="italic">I would not let him go.</hi> Not only, I would never do any thing to provoke him to depart, but I would by faith and prayer prevail with him to stay, and by the exercise of grace preserve inward peace." Those that know how hard comfort is come by, and how dearly it is bought, will be afraid of forfeiting it and playing it away, and will think nothing too much to do to keep it safe. <hi type="italic">Non minor est virtus quam quærere parta tueri</hi>—<hi type="italic">As much is implied in securing our acquisitions as in making them.</hi> Those that have laid hold on wisdom must <hi type="italic">retain her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Prov. iii. 18</reference>. Those that hold Christ fast in the arms of faith and love shall <hi type="italic">not let him go;</hi> he will abide with them. <div eID="gen15250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15251" type="x-p"/> VI. How desirous she was to make others acquainted with him: "<hi type="italic">I brought him to my mother's house,</hi> that all my relations, all who are dear to me, might have the benefit of communion with him." When Zaccheus found Christ, or rather was found of him, <hi type="italic">salvation came to his house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.9">Luke xix. 9</reference>. Wherever we find Christ we must take him home with us to our houses, especially to our hearts. The church is our mother, and we should be concerned for her interests, that she may have Christ present with her and be earnest in prayer for his presence with his people and ministers always. Those that enjoy the tokens of Christ's favour to their own souls should desire that the church, and all religious assemblies in their public capacity, might likewise enjoy the tokens of his favour. <div eID="gen15251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15252" type="x-p"/> VII. What care she was in that no disturbance might be given him (<reference osisRef="Song.3.5">v. 5</reference>); she repeats the charge she had before given (<reference osisRef="Song.2.7">ch. ii. 7</reference>) to the <hi type="italic">daughters of Jerusalem</hi> not to <hi type="italic">stir up or awake her love.</hi> When she <hi type="italic">had brought him into her mother's house,</hi> among her sisters, she gives them a strict charge to keep all quiet and in good order, to be very observant of him, careful to please him, and afraid of offending him. The charge given to the church in the wilderness concerning the angel of the covenant, who was among them, explains this. <reference osisRef="Exod.23.21">Exod. xxiii. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">Beware of him and obey his voice;</hi> <hi type="italic">provoke him not.</hi> See that none of you stir out of your places, lest you disturb him, but <hi type="italic">with quietness work and mind your own business;</hi> make no noise; let all <hi type="italic">clamour and bitterness be put</hi> far <hi type="italic">from you,</hi> for that <hi type="italic">grieves the Holy Spirit of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.30-Eph.4.31">Eph. iv. 30, 31</reference>. Some make this to be Christ's charge to the <hi type="italic">daughters of Jerusalem</hi> not to disturb or disquiet his church, nor trouble the minds of the disciples; for Christ is very tender of the peace of his church, and all the members of it, even the little ones; and those that trouble them <hi type="italic">shall bear their judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.5.10">Gal. v. 10</reference>.
entries.932d3c1ba2bf44424b15277f6f26e41462942c33: <div eID="gen15252" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15253" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> this that cometh out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all powders of the merchant? <div eID="gen15253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15254" type="x-p"/> These are the words of the <hi type="italic">daughters of Jerusalem,</hi> to whom the charge was given, <reference osisRef="Song.3.5">v. 5</reference>. They had looked shily upon the bride because she was black (<reference osisRef="Song.1.6">ch. i. 6</reference>); but now they admire her, and speak of her with great respect: <hi type="italic">Who is this?</hi> How beautiful she looks! Who would have expected such a comely and magnificent person to <hi type="italic">come out of the wilderness?</hi> As, when Christ rode in triumph into Jerusalem, they said, <hi type="italic">Who is this?</hi> And of the accession of strangers to the church she herself says, with wonder (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.21">Isa. xlix. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">Who has begotten me these?</hi> 1. This is applicable to the Jewish church, when, after forty years' wandering in the wilderness, they came out of it, to take a glorious possession of the land of promise; and this may very well be illustrated by what Balaam said of them at that time, when they ascended <hi type="italic">out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke,</hi> and he stood admiring them: <hi type="italic">From the top of the rocks I see him. How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob!</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.9">Num. xxiii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.24.5">xxiv. 5</reference>. 2. It is applicable to any public deliverance of the church of God, as particularly of Babylon, the Old-Testament and the New-Testament Babylon; then the church is <hi type="italic">like pillars of smoke,</hi> ascending upwards in devout affections, the incense of praise, from which, as from Noah's sacrifice, God <hi type="italic">smells a sweet savour;</hi> then she is amiable in the eyes of her friends, and her enemies too cannot but have a veneration for her, and <hi type="italic">worship at her feet, knowing that God has loved her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>. Sometimes the <hi type="italic">fear of the Jews</hi> was upon their neighbours, when they saw that <hi type="italic">God was with them of a truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.8.17">Esth. viii. 17</reference>. 3. It is applicable to the recovery of a gracious soul out of a state of desertion and despondency. (1.) She ascends <hi type="italic">out of the wilderness,</hi> the dry and barren land, where there is <hi type="italic">no way,</hi> where there is <hi type="italic">no water,</hi> where travellers are still in want and ever at a loss; here a poor soul may long be left to wander, but shall come up, at last, under the conduct of the Comforter. (2.) She comes up <hi type="italic">like pillars of smoke,</hi> like a cloud of incense ascending from the altar or the smoke of the burnt-offerings. This intimates a fire of pious and devout affections in the soul, whence this smoke arises, and the mounting of the soul heaven-ward in this smoke (as <reference osisRef="Judg.13.20">Judges xiii. 20</reference>), the heart lifted up to God in the heavens, <hi type="italic">as the sparks fly upward.</hi> Christ's return to the soul gives life to its devotion, and its communion with God is most reviving when it ascends <hi type="italic">out of a wilderness.</hi> (3.) She is <hi type="italic">perfumed with myrrh and frankincense.</hi> She is replenished with the graces of God's Spirit, which are as sweet spices, or as the holy incense, which, being now kindled by his gracious returns, sends forth a very fragrant smell. Her devotions being now peculiarly lively, she is not only acceptable to God, but amiable in the eyes of others also, who are ready to cry out with admiration, <hi type="italic">Who is this?</hi> What a monument of mercy is this! The graces and comforts with which she is <hi type="italic">perfumed</hi> are called the <hi type="italic">powders of the merchant,</hi> for they are far-fetched and dear-bought, by our Lord Jesus, that blessed merchant, who took a long voyage, and was at vast expense, no less than that of his own blood, to purchase them for us. They are not the products of our own soil, nor the growth of our own country; no, they are imported from the heavenly Canaan, the better country.
entries.a862ccc26431e9803d265586f74ffc9f36efa37d: <div eID="gen15254" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15255" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Behold his bed, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Solomon's; threescore valiant men <hi type="italic">are</hi> about it, of the valiant of Israel. <hi type="super">8</hi> They all hold swords, <hi type="italic">being</hi> expert in war: every man <hi type="italic">hath</hi> his sword upon his thigh because of fear in the night. <hi type="super">9</hi> King Solomon made himself a chariot of the wood of Lebanon. <hi type="super">10</hi> He made the pillars thereof <hi type="italic">of</hi> silver, the bottom thereof <hi type="italic">of</hi> gold, the covering of it <hi type="italic">of</hi> purple, the midst thereof being paved <hi type="italic">with</hi> love, for the daughters of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">11</hi> Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, and in the day of the gladness of his heart. <div eID="gen15255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15256" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">The daughters of Jerusalem</hi> stood admiring the spouse and commending her, but she overlooks their praises, is not puffed up with them, but transfers all the glory to Christ, and directs them to look off from her to him, recommends him to their esteem, and sets herself to applaud him. Here he is three times called <hi type="italic">Solomon,</hi> and we have that name but three times besides in all this song, <reference osisRef="Song.1.5">ch. i. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.8.11-Song.8.12">viii. 11, 12</reference>. It is Christ that is here meant, who is greater than Solomon, and of whom Solomon was an illustrious type for his wisdom and wealth, and especially his building the temple. <div eID="gen15256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15257" type="x-p"/> Three things she admires him for:— <div eID="gen15257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15258" type="x-p"/> I. The safety of his bed (<reference osisRef="Song.3.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold his bed,</hi> even <hi type="italic">Solomon's,</hi> very rich and fine; for such <hi type="italic">the curtains of Solomon</hi> were. <hi type="italic">His bed, which is above Solomon's,</hi> so some read it. Christ's bed, though he had <hi type="italic">not where to lay his head,</hi> is better than Solomon's best bed. The church is his bed, for he has said of it. <hi type="italic">This is my rest for ever;</hi> <hi type="italic">here will I dwell.</hi> The hearts of believers are his bed, for he lies all night between their breasts, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.17">Eph. iii. 17</reference>. Heaven is his bed, the rest into which he entered when he had done his work. Or it may be meant of the sweet repose and satisfaction which gracious souls enjoy in communion with him; it is called <hi type="italic">his bed,</hi> because, though we are admitted to it, and therefore it is called <hi type="italic">our bed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.1.16">ch. i. 16</reference>), yet it is his peace that is our rest, <reference osisRef="John.14.27">John xiv. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">I will give you rest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Matt. xi. 28</reference>. It <hi type="italic">is Solomon's bed,</hi> whose name signifies <hi type="italic">peace,</hi> because in his days Judah and Israel <hi type="italic">dwelt safely under their vines and fig-trees.</hi> That which she admires his bed for is the guard that surrounded it. Those that rest in Christ not only dwell at ease (many do so who yet are in the greatest danger) but they dwell in safety. Their holy serenity is under the protection of a holy security. This bed had <hi type="italic">threescore valiant men about it,</hi> as yeomen of the guard, or the band of gentlemen-pensioners; they are <hi type="italic">of the valiant of Israel,</hi> and a great many bold and brave men David's reign had produced. The life-guard men are well armed: <hi type="italic">They all hold swords,</hi> and know how to hold them; they are <hi type="italic">expert in war,</hi> well skilled in all the arts of it. They are posted about the bed at a convenient distance. They are in a posture of defence, <hi type="italic">every man</hi> with <hi type="italic">his sword upon his thigh</hi> and his hand upon his sword, ready to draw upon the first alarm, and this <hi type="italic">because of fear in the night,</hi> because of the danger feared; for the lives of princes, even the wisest and best, as they are more precious, so they are more exposed, and require to be more guarded than the lives of common persons. Or, <hi type="italic">because of the fear</hi> of it, and the apprehension which the spouse may have of danger, these guards are set for her satisfaction, that she may be <hi type="italic">quiet from the fear of evil,</hi> which believers themselves are subject to, especially <hi type="italic">in the night,</hi> when they are under a cloud as to their spiritual state, or in any outward trouble more than ordinary. Christ himself was under the special protection of his Father in his whole undertaking. <hi type="italic">In the shadow of his hand he hid me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Isa. xlix. 2</reference>); he had legions of angels at his command. The church is well guarded; more are with her than against her. Lest any hurt this vineyard, God himself <hi type="italic">keeps it night and day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.2-Isa.27.3">Isa. xxvii. 2, 3</reference>); particular believers, when they repose themselves in Christ and with him, though it may be night-time with them, and they may have their <hi type="italic">fears in the night,</hi> and yet safe, as safe as Solomon himself in the midst of his guards; the angels have a charge concerning them, ministers are appointed to <hi type="italic">watch for their souls,</hi> and <hi type="italic">they</hi> ought to be <hi type="italic">valiant</hi> men, <hi type="italic">expert in</hi> the spiritual warfare, holding <hi type="italic">the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,</hi> and having that girt <hi type="italic">upon their thigh,</hi> always ready to them for the silencing <hi type="italic">of the fears</hi> of God's people <hi type="italic">in the night.</hi> All the attributes of God are engaged for the safety of believers; they are kept as in a strong-hold by his power (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.5">1 Pet. i. 5</reference>), are safe in <hi type="italic">his name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Prov. xviii. 10</reference>), his peace protects those in whom it rules (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Phil. iv. 7</reference>), and the effect of righteousness in them is <hi type="italic">quietness</hi> and <hi type="italic">assurance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">Isa. xxxii. 17</reference>. Our danger is from <hi type="italic">the rulers of the darkness of this world,</hi> but we are safe in the <hi type="italic">armour of light.</hi> <div eID="gen15258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15259" type="x-p"/> II. The splendour of his chariot, <reference osisRef="Song.3.9-Song.3.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. As Christ and believers rest in safety under a sufficient guard, so when they appear publicly, as kings in their coaches of state, they appear in great magnificence. This chariot was of Solomon's own contriving and making, the materials very rich, <hi type="italic">silver,</hi> and <hi type="italic">gold,</hi> and <hi type="italic">cedar,</hi> and <hi type="italic">purple.</hi> He made it for himself, and yet made it <hi type="italic">for the daughters of Jerusalem,</hi> to oblige them. Some by this <hi type="italic">chariot,</hi> or <hi type="italic">coach,</hi> or <hi type="italic">chaise</hi> (the word is nowhere else used in scripture), understand the human nature of Christ, in which the divine nature rode as in an open chariot. It was a divine workmanship (<hi type="italic">A body hast thou prepared me</hi>); the structure was very fine, but that which was at the bottom of it was love, pure love to the children of men. Others make it to represent the everlasting gospel, in which, as in an open chariot, Christ shows himself, and as in a chariot of war rides forth triumphantly, <hi type="italic">conquering and to conquer. The pillars,</hi> the seven pillars (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.1">Prov. ix. 1</reference>), are of <hi type="italic">silver,</hi> for the words of the Lord are <hi type="italic">as silver tried</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Ps. xii. 6</reference>), nay, they are better <hi type="italic">than thousands of gold and silver.</hi> It is hung with <hi type="italic">purple,</hi> a princely colour; all the adornings of it are dyed in the precious blood of Christ, and that gives them this colour. But that which completes the glory of it is <hi type="italic">love;</hi> <hi type="italic">it is paved with love,</hi> it is lined with love, not love of strangers, as Solomon's was in the days of his defection, but <hi type="italic">love</hi> of <hi type="italic">the daughters of Jerusalem,</hi> a holy <hi type="italic">love.</hi> Silver is better than cedar, gold than silver, but love is better than gold, better than all, and it is put last, for nothing can be better than that. The gospel is all <hi type="italic">love.</hi> Mr. Durham applies it to the covenant of redemption, the way of our salvation, as it is contrived in the eternal counsel of God, and manifested to us in the scriptures. This is that work of Christ himself wherein the glory of his grace and love to sinners most eminently appears, and which makes him amiable and admirable in the eyes of believers. In this covenant love is conveyed to them, and they are carried in it to the perfection of love, and, as it were, ride in triumph. It is admirably framed and contrived, both for the glory of Christ and for the comfort of believers. It is <hi type="italic">well ordered in all things, and sure</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2 Sam. xxiii. 5</reference>); it has <hi type="italic">pillars</hi> that cannot be shaken, it is <hi type="italic">made of the wood of Lebanon,</hi> which can never rot; the basis of it is <hi type="italic">gold,</hi> the most lasting metal; the blood of the covenant, that rich <hi type="italic">purple,</hi> is the cover of this chariot, by which believers are sheltered from the wind and storms of divine wrath, and the troubles of this world; but the midst of it, and that which is all in all in it, is <hi type="italic">love,</hi> that <hi type="italic">love of Christ which surpasses knowledge</hi> and the dimensions of which are immeasurable. <div eID="gen15259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15260" type="x-p"/> III. The lustre of his royal person, when he appears in his greatest pomp, <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">v. 11</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen15260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15261" type="x-p"/> 1. The call that is given to the <hi type="italic">daughters of Zion</hi> to acquaint themselves with the glories of <hi type="italic">king Solomon: Go forth, and behold</hi> him. The multitude of the spectators adds to the beauty of a splendid cavalcade. Christ, in his gospel, manifests himself. Let each of us add to the number of those that give honour to him, by giving themselves the satisfaction of looking upon him. Who should pay respects to Zion's king but Zion's daughters? They have reason to rejoice greatly when he comes, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec. ix. 9</reference>. (1.) <hi type="italic">Behold him</hi> then. Look with pleasure upon Christ in his glory. Look upon him with an eye of faith, with a fixed eye. Here is a sight worth seeing; <hi type="italic">behold,</hi> and admire him, <hi type="italic">behold,</hi> and love him; look upon him, and know him again. (2.) <hi type="italic">Go forth and behold</hi> him; go off from the world, as those that see no beauty and excellency in it in comparison with what is to be seen in the Lord Jesus. Go out of yourselves, and let the light of his transcendent beauty put you out of conceit with yourselves. <hi type="italic">Go forth</hi> to the place where he is to be seen, to the street through which he passes, as Zaccheus. <div eID="gen15261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15262" type="x-p"/> 2. The direction that is given them to take special notice of that which they would not see every day, and that was his <hi type="italic">crown,</hi> either the crown of gold, adorned with jewels, which he wore on his coronation-day (Solomon's mother, Bathsheba, though she did not procure that for him, yet, by her seasonable interposal, she helped to secure it to him when Adonijah was catching at it), or the garland or crown of flowers and green tied with ribbons which his mother made for him, to adorn the solemnity of his nuptials. Perhaps Solomon's coronation day was his marriage-day, <hi type="italic">the day of his espousals,</hi> when the garland his mother crowned him with was added to the crown his people crowned him with. Applying this to Christ, it speaks, (1.) The many honours put upon him, and the power and dominion he is entrusted with: <hi type="italic">Go forth,</hi> and see king Jesus, <hi type="italic">with the crown wherewith his</hi> Father <hi type="italic">crowned him,</hi> when he declared him his <hi type="italic">beloved Son, in whom</hi> he was <hi type="italic">well-pleased,</hi> when he <hi type="italic">set him as King upon his holy hill of Zion,</hi> when he advanced him to his own right hand, and invested him with a sovereign authority, both <hi type="italic">in heaven and in earth,</hi> and <hi type="italic">put all things under his feet.</hi> (2.) The dishonour put upon him by his persecutors. Some apply it to the <hi type="italic">crown of thorns</hi> with which <hi type="italic">his mother,</hi> the Jewish church, <hi type="italic">crowned him</hi> on the day of his death, which was <hi type="italic">the day of his espousals</hi> to his church, when he <hi type="italic">loved it, and gave himself for it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.25">Eph. v. 25</reference>); and it is observable that when he was <hi type="italic">brought forth wearing the crown of thorns Pilate said,</hi> and said it to the <hi type="italic">daughters of Zion, Behold the man.</hi> (3.) It seems especially to mean the honour done him by his church, as his mother, and by all true believers, in whose hearts he is formed, and of whom he has said, <hi type="italic">These are my mother, my sister, and brother,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.12.50">Matt. xii. 50</reference>. They give him the glory of his undertaking; to him is glory <hi type="italic">in the church,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.21">Eph. iii. 21</reference>. When believers accept of him as theirs, and join themselves to him in an everlasting covenant, [1.] It is his coronation-day in their souls. Before conversion they were crowning themselves, but then they begin to crown Christ, and continue to do so from that day forward. They appointed him their head; they bring <hi type="italic">every thought into obedience to</hi> him; they set up his throne in their hearts, and cast all their crowns at his feet. [2.] It is <hi type="italic">the day of his espousals,</hi> in which he betroths them to him for ever in lovingkindness and in mercies, joins them to himself in faith and love, and gives himself to them in the promises and all he has, to be theirs. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not be for another, so will I also be for thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.3.3">Hos. iii. 3</reference>. And to him they are presented as <hi type="italic">chaste virgins.</hi> [3.] It is <hi type="italic">the day of the gladness of his heart;</hi> he is pleased with the honour that his people do him, pleased with the progress of his interest among them. Does <hi type="italic">Satan fall</hi> before them? <hi type="italic">In that hour Jesus rejoices in spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.10.18">Luke x. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.10.21">21</reference>. There is joy in heaven over repenting sinners; the family is glad when the prodigal son returns. <hi type="italic">Go forth and behold</hi> Christ's grace toward sinners, as his <hi type="italic">crown,</hi> his brightest glory.  <chapter eID="Song.3"/> <div eID="gen15262" type="x-p"/>

entries.2c6c225664ee5d96952b3feaf6b88d0f37182ae0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8226"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen12934" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Song.3.1-Song.3.11">So 3:1-11</reference>.<div eID="gen12934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12935" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8226"/><hi type="bold">1. By night--</hi>literally, "By nights." Continuation of the longing for the dawn of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Song.2.17">So 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.130.6">Psa 130:6</reference>; Mal 4:2). The spiritual desertion here (<reference osisRef="Song.2.17">So 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">3:5</reference>) is not due to indifference, as in <reference osisRef="Song.5.2-Song.5.8">So 5:2-8</reference>. "As nights and dews are better for flowers than a continual sun, so Christ's absence (at times) giveth sap to humility, and putteth an edge on hunger, and furnisheth a fair field to faith to put forth itself" [Rutherford]. Contrast <reference osisRef="Song.1.13">So 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.30.6">Psa 30:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.7">7</reference>.<div eID="gen12935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on ... bed--</hi>the secret of her failure (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.7">Is 64:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.13">Jr 29:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.7.14">Ho 7:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loveth--</hi>no want of sincerity, but of diligence, which she now makes up for by leaving her bed to seek Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.2">Psa 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.63.8">63:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Is 26:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.17">Joh 20:17</reference>). Four times (<reference osisRef="Song.3.1-Song.3.4">So 3:1-4</reference>) she calls Jesus Christ, "Him whom my soul loveth," designating Him as absent; language of desire: "He loved me," would be language of present fruition (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>). In questioning the watchmen (<reference osisRef="Song.3.3">So 3:3</reference>), she does not even name Him, so full is her heart of Him. Having found Him at dawn (for throughout He is the morning), she charges the daughters not to abridge by intrusion the period of His stay. Compare as to the thoughtful seeking for Jesus Christ in the time of John the Baptist, in vain at first, but presently after successful (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.15-Luke.3.22">Lu 3:15-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.19-John.1.34">Joh 1:19-34</reference>).<div eID="gen12937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">found him not--</hi>Oh, for such honest dealings with ourselves (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.14">Pr 25:14</reference>; Jude 12)! <div eID="gen12938" type="x-p"/>
entries.0205e81c2455d2e870d188df6b22e8d18a16691c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8227"/><div sID="gen12939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8227"/><hi type="bold">2. Wholly awake for God (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.18-Luke.14.20">Lu 14:18-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Ep 5:14</reference>). "An honest resolution is often to (the doing of) duty, like a needle that draws the thread after it" [Durham]. Not a mere wish, that counts not the cost--</hi>to leave her easy bed, and wander in the dark night seeking Him (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.4">Pr 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.30">Mt 21:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.14.27-Luke.14.33">Lu 14:27-33</reference>).<div eID="gen12939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the city--</hi>Jerusalem, literally (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.5">Mt 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.19">Joh 1:19</reference>), and spiritually the Church here (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>), in glory (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Re 21:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">broad ways--</hi>open spaces at the gates of Eastern cities, where the public assembled for business. So, the assemblies of worshippers (<reference osisRef="Song.8.2">So 8:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.8.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20-Prov.1.23">Pr 1:20-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">He 10:25</reference>). She had in her first awakening shrunk from them, seeking Jesus Christ alone; but she was desired to seek the footsteps of the flock (<reference osisRef="Song.1.8">So 1:8</reference>), so now in her second trial she goes forth to them of herself. "The more the soul grows in grace, and the less it leans on ordinances, the more it prizes and profits by them" [Moody Stuart] (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.16">Psa 73:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen12941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">found him not--</hi>Nothing short of Jesus Christ can satisfy her (<reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.10">Job 23:8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1">Psa 63:1</reference>, 2). <div eID="gen12942" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2d0d9c37fd17eeed8c09c0e032966e0a9e779d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8228"/><div sID="gen12943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8228"/><hi type="bold">3. watchmen--</hi>ministers (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">Jr 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.17">Eze 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">He 13:17</reference>), fit persons to consult (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.11">Is 21:11</reference>; Mal 2:7).<div eID="gen12943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">found me--</hi>the general ministry of the Word "finds" individually souls in quest of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.27">Ge 24:27</reference>, end of verse <reference osisRef="Acts.16.14">Ac 16:14</reference>); whereas formalists remain unaffected. <div eID="gen12944" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2b040db8ef260002eb694eaf401caf01576f755: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8229"/><div sID="gen12945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8229"/>4. Jesus Christ is generally "found" near the watchmen and means of grace; but they are not Himself; the star that points to Beth-lehem is not the Sun that has risen there; she hastens past the guideposts to the goal [Moody Stuart]. Not even angels could satisfy Mary, instead of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="John.20.11-John.20.16">Joh 20:11-16</reference>).<div eID="gen12945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">found him--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Is 45:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1-Hos.6.3">Ho 6:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.44-Matt.13.46">Mt 13:44-46</reference>).<div eID="gen12946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">held him, &c.--</hi>willing to be held; not willing, if not held (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.26">Ge 32:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.9">Mt 28:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.24.28">Lu 24:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.11">Re 3:11</reference>). "As a little weeping child will hold its mother fast, not because it is stronger than she, but because her bowels constrain her not to leave it; so Jesus Christ yearning over the believer cannot go, because He will not" [Durham]. In <reference osisRef="Song.1.4">So 1:4</reference> it is He who leads the bride into His chambers; here it is she who leads Him into her mother's. There are times when the grace of Jesus Christ seems to draw us to Him; and others, when we with strong cries draw Him to us and ours. In the East one large apartment often serves for the whole family; so the bride here speaks of her mother's apartment and her own together. The mention of the "mother" excludes impropriety, and imparts the idea of heavenly love, pure as a sister's, while ardent as a bride's; hence the frequent title, "my sister--spouse." Our mother after the Spirit, is the Church, the new Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="John.3.5-John.3.8">Joh 3:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.19">Ga 4:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">26</reference>); for her we ought to pray continually (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.14-Eph.3.19">Ep 3:14-19</reference>), also for the national Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.1">Ro 10:1</reference>), also for the human family, which is our mother and kindred after the flesh; these our mother's children have evilly treated us (<reference osisRef="Song.1.6">So 1:6</reference>); but, like our Father, we are to return good for evil (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Mt 5:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">45</reference>), and so bring Jesus Christ home to them (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.12">1Pe 2:12</reference>). <div eID="gen12947" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7bbdcba9838beee2aad65778b54425b04b0e307: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8230"/><div sID="gen12948" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8230"/>5. So <reference osisRef="Song.2.7">So 2:7</reference>; but there it was for the non-interruption of her own fellowship with Jesus Christ that she was anxious; here it is for the not grieving of the Holy Ghost, on the part of the daughters of Jerusalem. Jealously avoid levity, heedlessness, and offenses which would mar the gracious work begun in others (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.7">Mt 18:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.42">Ac 2:42</reference>, 43; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.30">Ep 4:30</reference>).<div eID="gen12948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Canticle III.--</hi>(So 3:6-5:1)--The Bridegroom with the Bride.<div eID="gen12949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12950" type="x-p"/> Historically, the ministry of Jesus Christ on earth. <div eID="gen12950" type="x-p"/>
entries.a11c872297fad68ae289e1c1aa060143ad338514: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8231"/><div sID="gen12951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8231"/>6. New scene (<reference osisRef="Song.3.6-Song.3.11">So 3:6-11</reference>). The friends of the Bridegroom see a cortege approach. His palanquin and guard.<div eID="gen12951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cometh out--</hi>rather, "up from"; the wilderness was lower than Jerusalem [Maurer].<div eID="gen12952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12953" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pillars of smoke--</hi>from the perfumes burned around Him and His bride. Image from Israel and the tabernacle (answering to "bed," <reference osisRef="Song.3.7">So 3:7</reference>) marching through the desert with the pillar of smoke by day and fire by night (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.20">Ex 14:20</reference>), and the pillars of smoke ascending from the altars of incense and of atonement; so Jesus Christ's righteousness, atonement, and ever-living intercession. Balaam, the last representative of patriarchism, was required to curse the Jewish Church, just as it afterwards would not succumb to Christianity without a struggle (<reference osisRef="Num.22.41">Nu 22:41</reference>), but he had to bless in language like that here (<reference osisRef="Num.24.5">Nu 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.6">6</reference>). Angels too joyfully ask the same question, when Jesus Christ with the tabernacle of His body (answering to "His bed," <reference osisRef="Song.3.7">So 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>, "dwelt," Greek "tabernacled," <reference osisRef="John.2.21">Joh 2:21</reference>) ascends into heaven (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.8-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:8-10</reference>); also when they see His glorious bride with Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Psa 68:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.13-Rev.7.17">Re 7:13-17</reference>). Encouragement to her; amid the darkest trials (<reference osisRef="Song.3.1">So 3:1</reference>), she is still on the road to glory (<reference osisRef="Song.3.11">So 3:11</reference>) in a palanquin "paved with love" (<reference osisRef="Song.3.10">So 3:10</reference>); she is now in soul spiritually "coming," exhaling the sweet graces, faith, love, joy, peace, prayer, and praise; (the fire is lighted within, the "smoke" is seen without, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.13">Ac 4:13</reference>); it is in the desert of trial (<reference osisRef="Song.3.1-Song.3.3">So 3:1-3</reference>) she gets them; she is the "merchant" buying from Jesus Christ without money or price (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Is 55:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Re 3:18</reference>); just as myrrh and frankincense are got, not in Egypt, but in the Arabian sands and the mountains of Palestine. Hereafter she shall "come" (<reference osisRef="Song.3.6">So 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">11</reference>) in a glorified body, too (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Php 3:21</reference>). Historically, Jesus Christ returning from the wilderness, full of the Holy Ghost (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.1">Lu 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.14">14</reference>). The same, "Who is this," &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Is 63:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">5</reference>). <div eID="gen12953" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ea29f973c8552fed32babbb992dbb65c4ae0d48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8232"/><div sID="gen12954" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8232"/>7. In <reference osisRef="Song.3.6">So 3:6</reference> the wilderness character of the Church is portrayed; in <reference osisRef="Song.3.7">So 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.3.8">8</reference>, its militant aspect. In <reference osisRef="Song.3.9">So 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.3.10">10</reference>, Jesus Christ is seen dwelling in believers, who are His "chariot" and "body." In <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">So 3:11</reference>, the consummation in glory.<div eID="gen12954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bed--</hi>palanquin. His body, literally, guarded by a definite number of angels, threescore, or sixty (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.53">Mt 26:53</reference>), from the wilderness (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.1">Mt 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.11">11</reference>), and continually (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.13">Lu 2:13</reference>; 22:43; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.10">Ac 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>); just as six hundred thousand of Israel guarded the Lord's tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Num.2.17-Num.2.32">Nu 2:17-32</reference>), one for every ten thousand. In contrast to the "bed of sloth" (<reference osisRef="Song.3.1">So 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen12955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">valiant--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Josh.5.13">Jos 5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.5.14">14</reference>). Angels guarding His tomb used like words (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.6">Mr 16:6</reference>).<div eID="gen12956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Israel--</hi>true subjects, not mercenaries. <div eID="gen12957" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a073fcf8b7db2531d4641ceb3b764856b4d2a76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8233"/><div sID="gen12958" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8233"/><hi type="bold">8. hold--</hi>not actually grasping them, but having them girt on the thigh ready for use, like their Lord (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.3">Psa 45:3</reference>). So believers too are guarded by angels (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.11">Psa 91:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">He 1:14</reference>), and they themselves need "every man" (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.18">Ne 4:18</reference>) to be armed (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.1">Psa 144:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4">2Co 10:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.12">1Ti 6:12</reference>), and "expert" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">2Co 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen12958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12959" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of fear in the night--</hi>Arab marauders often turn a wedding into mourning by a night attack. So the bridal procession of saints in the night of this wilderness is the chief object of Satan's assault. <div eID="gen12959" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc45f2e38676ea9cc832c1cf7859c79ac724f367: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8234"/><div sID="gen12960" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8234"/><hi type="bold">9. chariot--</hi>more elaborately made than the "bed" or travelling litter (<reference osisRef="Song.3.7">So 3:7</reference>), from a Hebrew root, "to elaborate" [Ewald]. So the temple of "cedar of Lebanon," as compared with the temporary tabernacle of shittim wood (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.2">2Sa 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.7">6, 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.14">1Ki 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.15-1Kgs.6.18">6:15-18</reference>), Jesus Christ's body is the antitype, "made" by the Father for Him (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">He 10:5</reference>), the wood answering to His human nature, the gold, His divine; the two being but one Christ. <div eID="gen12960" type="x-p"/>
entries.f311e9276da704f098fcf75e662dd22f57a9eba8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8235"/><div sID="gen12961" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8235"/><hi type="bold">10. pillars--</hi>supporting the canopy at the four corners; curtains at the side protect the person within from the sun. Pillars with silver sockets supported the veil that enclosed the holy of holies; emblem of Jesus Christ's strength (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.21">1Ki 7:21</reference>), Margin, "silver," emblem of His purity (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Psa 12:6</reference>); so the saints hereafter (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Re 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen12961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12962" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bottom--</hi>rather, "the back for resting or reclining on" (Vulgate and Septuagint) [Maurer]. So the floor and mercy seat, the resting-place of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">Psa 132:14</reference>) in the temple, was gold (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.30">1Ki 6:30</reference>).<div eID="gen12962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covering--</hi>rather, "seat," as in <reference osisRef="Lev.15.9">Le 15:9</reference>. Hereafter the saints shall share His seat (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Re 3:21</reference>).<div eID="gen12963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12964" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purple--</hi>the veil of the holiest, partly purple, and the purple robe put on Jesus Christ, accord with English Version, "covering." "Purple" (including scarlet and crimson) is the emblem of royalty, and of His blood; typified by the passover lamb's blood, and the wine when the twelve sat or reclined at the Lord's table.<div eID="gen12964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">paved--</hi>translated, like mosaic pavement, with the various acts and promises of love of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zep 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.8">1Jo 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.4.16">16</reference>), in contrast with the tables of stone in the "midst" of the ark, covered with writings of stern command (compare <reference osisRef="John.19.13">Joh 19:13</reference>); this is all grace and love to believers, who answer to "the daughters of Jerusalem" (<reference osisRef="John.1.17">Joh 1:17</reference>). The exterior silver and gold, cedar, purple, and guards, may deter, but when the bride enters within, she rests on a pavement of love. <div eID="gen12965" type="x-p"/>
entries.350b3f0ecdea86fee9912ac7766e3b1a7eaf61af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8236"/><div sID="gen12966" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8236"/><hi type="bold">11. Go forth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.25.6">Mt 25:6</reference>).<div eID="gen12966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughters of Zion--</hi>spirits of saints, and angels (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crown--</hi>nuptial (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.8-Ezek.16.12">Eze 16:8-12</reference>), (the Hebrews wore costly crowns or chaplets at weddings), and kingly (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.12">Re 19:12</reference>). The crown of thorns was once His nuptial chaplet, His blood the wedding wine cup (<reference osisRef="John.19.5">Joh 19:5</reference>). "His mother," that so crowned Him, is the human race, for He is "the Son of man," not merely the son of Mary. The same mother reconciled to Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.50">Mt 12:50</reference>), as the Church, travails in birth for souls, which she presents to Him as a crown (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.1">Php 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.4.10">Re 4:10</reference>). Not being ashamed to call the children brethren (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.11-Heb.2.14">He 2:11-14</reference>), He calls their mother His mother (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.9">Psa 22:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Ro 8:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.1">Re 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2</reference>).<div eID="gen12968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12969" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.10">2Th 1:10</reference>).<div eID="gen12969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day of his espousals--</hi>chiefly the final marriage, when the number of the elect is complete (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.11">Re 6:11</reference>).<div eID="gen12970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gladness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.45.15">Psa 45:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">Is 62:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Re 19:7</reference>). Moody Stuart observes as to this Canticle (So 3:6-5:1), the center of the Book, these characteristics: (1) The bridegroom takes the chief part, whereas elsewhere the bride is the chief speaker. (2) Elsewhere He is either "King" or "Solomon"; here He is twice called "King Solomon." The bride is six times here called the "spouse"; never so before or after; also "sister" four times, and, except in the first verse of the next Canticle [So 5:2], nowhere else. (3) He and she are never separate; no absence, no complaint, which abound elsewhere, are in this Canticle. <chapter eID="Song.3"/>

entries.d271917460d9b1ecf286ef57c1568e59b801ab83: <div eID="gen25967" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25968" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25969" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25969" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25968" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25970" type="x-p"/> The bride mentions the absence of her spouse, her search after him, and her ultimate success, <reference osisRef="Sol.3.1-Sol.3.5">Sol 3:1-5</reference>. A description of the bridegroom, his bed, chariot, etc., <reference osisRef="Sol.3.6-Sol.3.11">Sol 3:6-11</reference>. <div eID="gen25970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25971" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25972" type="x-p"/> By night on my bed I sought him - It appears that the bridegroom only saw the bride by night: that on the night referred to here he did not come as usual. The bride troubled on the account, rose and sought him, inquired of the city guards, and continued to seek till at last she found him, and brought him to her apartment, <reference osisRef="Sol.3.2-Sol.3.4">Sol 3:2-4</reference>.
entries.6a42ad920502cce2d4b6f15c956418f3d2b480fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen25972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25973" type="x-p"/> Into my mother's house - The women in the East have all separate apartments, into which no person ever attempts to enter except the husband. We find Isaac bringing Rebecca into his mother's tent, when he made her his wife, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.67">Gen 24:67</reference>. What is here related appears to refer to the third night of the nuptials.
entries.8d808e60f2485b57a887ddbe428b62cee446b451: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen25973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25974" type="x-p"/> I charge you - The same adjuration as before, <reference osisRef="Sol.2.7">Sol 2:7</reference>.
entries.980844709de8560a5bb5dba4e027ff8f81e23946: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen25974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25975" type="x-p"/> Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness - Going to Egypt was called descending or going down, coming from it was termed coming up. The bride, having risen, goes after her spouse to the country, and the clouds of incense arising from her palanquin seemed like pillars of smoke; and the appearance was altogether so splendid as to attract the admiration of her own women, who converse about her splendor, excellence, etc., and then take occasion to describe Solomon's nuptial bed and chariot. Some think that it is the bridegroom who is spoken of here. With this verse the third night is supposed to end.
entries.7d4ae3fa773ac02939c85611dff274aa4c377107: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen25975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25976" type="x-p"/> Threescore valiant men - These were the guards about the pavilion of the bridegroom, who were placed there because of fear in the night. The security and state of the prince required such a guard as this, and the passage is to be literally understood.
entries.68e08bf5e992e71ebf82800fd6e9f1f76de31376: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen25976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25977" type="x-p"/> They all hold swords - They are swordsmen. Every man has a sword, and is well instructed how to use it.
entries.06362626dd933ca39b483fc74c6901edf9d26c86: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen25977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25978" type="x-p"/> Of the wood of Lebanon - Of the cedar that grew on that mount. It is very likely that a nuptial bed, not a chariot, is intended by the original word אפיון appiryon. Montanus properly translates it sponsarum thalamum, a nuptial bed. It may, however, mean a palanquin.
entries.40a146be4be8e46e8d600b079382cf6f00f3de1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen25978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25979" type="x-p"/> The pillars - of silver - The bedposts were made of silver, or cased with wrought silver plates, like the king's chairs brought from Hanover, now, in one of the staterooms in Windsor Castle. <div eID="gen25979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25980" type="x-p"/> The bottom thereof of gold - This may refer to cords made of gold thread, or to the mattress, which was made of cloth ornamented with gold. <div eID="gen25980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25981" type="x-p"/> The covering - of purple - Most probably the canopy. <div eID="gen25981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25982" type="x-p"/> The midst - paved with love - The counterpane, a superb piece of embroidery, wrought by some of the noble maids of Jerusalem, and, as a proof of their affection, respect, and love, presented to the bride and bridegroom, on their nuptial day. This is most likely to be the sense of the passage, though some suppose it to refer to the whole court. <div eID="gen25982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25983" type="x-p"/> A Turkish couch is made of wooden lattices painted and gilded; the inside is painted with baskets of flowers and nosegays, intermixed with little mottoes according to the fancy of the artist. Solomon's couch may have been of the same kind, and decorated in the same way; and the paving with love may refer to the amatory verses worked either on the counterpane, hangings, or embroidered carpet. And as this was done by the daughters of Jerusalem, they might have expressed the most striking parts of such a chaste history of love as Halaly's Leely and Mejnoon on the different parts. I see that Dr. Good is of this opinion. It is sufficiently probable.
entries.bc8a9f5e4bf6065051b4e104e7d290b62aa77cbc: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen25983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25984" type="x-p"/> Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion - This is the exhortation of the companions of the bride to the females of the city to examine the superb appearance of the bridegroom, and especially the nuptial crown, which appears to have been made by Bathsheba, who it is supposed might have lived till the time of Solomon's marriage with the daughter of Pharaoh. It is conjectured that the prophet refers to a nuptial crown, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Isa 61:10</reference>. But a crown, both on the bride and bridegroom, was common among most people on such occasions. The nuptial crown among the Greeks and Romans was only a chaplet or wreath of flowers. <div eID="gen25984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25985" type="x-p"/> In the day of the gladness of his heart - The day in which all his wishes were crowned, by being united to that female whom beyond all others he loved. <div eID="gen25985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25986" type="x-p"/> Here the third day is supposed to end.  <chapter eID="Song.3"/> <div eID="gen25986" type="x-p"/>

entries.aa47db2ae4428106d409a2644aad1a0b9db1e69d: Sol 3:1 1 On my bed in the nights    I sought him whom my soul loveth:    I sought him, and found him not. <div eID="gen12552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12553" type="x-p"/> She does not mean to say that she sought him beside herself on her couch; for how could that be of the modest one, whose home-bringing is first described in the next act - she could and might miss him there neither waking nor sleeping. The commencement is like Job 33:15. She was at night on her couch, when a painful longing seized her: the beloved of her soul appeared to have forsaken her, to have withdrawn from her; she had lost the feeling of his nearness, and was not able to recover it. לילות is neither here nor at Sol 3:8 necessarily the categ. plur. The meaning may also be, that this pain, arising from a sense of being forgotten, always returned upon her for several nights through: she became distrustful of his fidelity; but the more she apprehended that she was no longer loved, the more ardent became her longing, and she arose to seek for him who had disappeared.
entries.79747f4dbc4672a6f652a59a070e568b16327dc6: Sol 3:2 2 So I will arise, then, and go about the city,    The markets, and the streets;    I will seek him whom my soul loveth! -    I sought him, and found him not. <div eID="gen12553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12554" type="x-p"/> How could this night-search, with all the strength of love, be consistent with the modesty of a maiden? It is thus a dream which she relates. And if the beloved of her soul were a shepherd, would she seek him in the city, and not rather without, in the field or in some village? No; the beloved of her soul is Solomon; and in the dream, Jerusalem, his city is transported close to the mountains of her native home. The resolution expressed by “I will arise, then,” is not introduced by “then I said,” or any similar phrase: the scene consists of a monologue which dramatically represents that which is experienced. Regarding the second <hi type="italic">Chatef-Pathach</hi> of ואס, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, p. 7. שׁוקים is the plur of שׁוּק (= shavḳ), as שׁורים of שׁוּר (= shavr); the root-word שוק (Arab. shaḳ) signifies to press on, to follow after continuously; (Arab.) suwaḳ designates perhaps, originally, the place to which one drives cattle for sale, as in the desert; (Arab.) sawaḳ designates the place to which one drives cattle for drink (Wetzst.). The form אבקשׁה is without the <hi type="italic">Daghesh</hi>, as are all the forms of this verb except the imper.; the semi-guttural nature of the <hi type="italic">Koph</hi> has something opposing the simple <hi type="italic">Sheva</hi>.
entries.5fc336341e4fd18f40f842c061bcd92ccc196704: Sol 3:3 <div eID="gen12554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12555" type="x-p"/> Shulamith now relates what she further experienced when, impelled by love-sorrow, she wandered through the city: 3 The watchmen who go about in the city found me:    “Have ye seen him whom my soul loveth?” <div eID="gen12555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12556" type="x-p"/> Here also (as in Sol 3:2) there is wanting before the question such a phrase as, “and I asked them, saying:” the monologue relates dramatically. If she described an outward experience, then the question would be a foolish one; for how could she suppose that the watchmen, who make their rounds in the city (Epstein, against Grätz, points for the antiquity of the order to <reference osisRef="Ps.127.1">Psa 127:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Isa 62:6</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.21.11">Isa 21:11</reference>), could have any knowledge of her beloved! But if she relates a dream, it is to be remembered that feeling and imagination rise higher than reflection. It is in the very nature of a dream, also, that things thus quickly follow one another without fixed lineaments. This also, that having gone out by night, she found in the streets him whom she sought, is a happy combination of circumstances formed in the dreaming soul; an occurrence without probable external reality, although not without deep inner truth:
entries.9165c14483ffebdbb754fc56ea97ab553220511d: Sol 3:4 4 Scarcely had I passed from them,    When I found him whom my soul loveth.    I seized him, and did not let him go    Until I brought him into the house of my mother,    And into the chamber of her that gave me birth. כּמעט = <hi type="italic">paululum</hi>, here standing for a sentence: it was as a little that I passed, etc. Without שׁ, it would be <hi type="italic">paululum transii</hi>; with it, <hi type="italic">paululum fuit quod transii</hi>, without any other distinction than that in the latter case the <hi type="italic">paululum</hi> is more emphatic. Since Shulamith relates something experienced earlier, אחזתּי is not fitly rendered by <hi type="italic">teneo</hi>, but by <hi type="italic">tenui</hi>; and ארפּנּוּ dna ;iune לאו, not by <hi type="italic">et non dimittam eum</hi>, but, as the neg. of וארפנו, <hi type="italic">et dimisi eum</hi>, - not merely <hi type="italic">et non dimittebam eum</hi>, but <hi type="italic">et non dimisi eum</hi>. In <reference osisRef="Gen.32.27">Gen 32:27</reference> [26], we read the cogn. שׁלּח, which signifies, to let go (“let me go”), as הרפּה, to let loose, to let free. It is all the same whether we translate, with the subjective colouring, <hi type="italic">donec introduxerim</hi>, or, with the objective, <hi type="italic">donec introduxi</hi>; in either case the meaning is that she held him fast till she brought him, by gentle violence, into her mother’s house. With בּית there is the more definite parallel חדר lellar, which properly signifies (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Sol 1:4), <hi type="italic">recessus</hi>, <hi type="italic">penetrale</hi>; with אמּי, the seldom occurring (only, besides, at Hos 2:7) הורה, <hi type="italic">part.f. Kal</hi> of הרה fo la, to conceive, be pregnant, which poetically, with the accus., may mean <hi type="italic">parturire</hi> or <hi type="italic">parere</hi>. In Jacob’s blessing, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.26">Gen 49:26</reference>, as the text lies before us, his parents are called הורי; just as in Arab. ummâni, properly “my two mothers,” may be used for “my parents;” in the Lat. also, <hi type="italic">parentes</hi> means father and mother zeugmatically taken together.
entries.20a89385dfa5b9b4c44d824f67d84dd2256804c7: Sol 3:5 <div eID="gen12556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12557" type="x-p"/> The closing words of the monologue are addressed to the daughters of Jerusalem. 5 I adjure you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem,    By the gazelles or the hinds of the field,    That ye awake not and disturb not love    Till she pleases. <div eID="gen12557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12558" type="x-p"/> We are thus obliged apparently to think of the daughters of Jerusalem as being present during the relation of the dream. But since Shulamith in the following Act is for the first time represented as brought from her home to Jerusalem, it is more probable that she represented her experience to herself in secret, without any auditors, and feasting on the visions of the dream, which brought her beloved so near, that she had him by herself alone and exclusively, that she fell into such a love-ecstasy as Sol 2:7; and pointing to the distant Jerusalem, deprecates all disturbance of this ecstasy, which in itself is like a slumber pervaded by pleasant dreams. In two monologues dramatically constructed, the poet has presented to us a view of the thoughts and feelings by which the inner life of the maiden was moved in the near prospect of becoming a bride and being married. Whoever reads the Song in the sense in which it is incorporated with the canon, and that, too, in the historical sense fulfilled in the N.T., will not be able to read the two scenes from Shulamith’s experience without finding therein a mirror of the intercourse of the soul with God in Christ, and cherishing thoughts such, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, as are expressed in the ancient hymn:<hi type="italic">Quando tandem venies, meus amor? Propera de Libano, dulcis amor! Clamat, amat sponsula: Veni, Jesu, Dulcis veni Jesu!</hi>
entries.a0676087b21580d6c03ab0159dadd165fa7e2c1f: Sol 3:6 6 Who is this coming up from the wilderness    Like pillars of smoke,    Perfumed with myrrh and frankincense,    With all aromatics of the merchants? <div eID="gen12558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12559" type="x-p"/> It is possible that זאת and עלה may be connected; but עני זה, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.7">Psa 34:7</reference> (this poor man, properly, this, a poor man), is not analogous, it ought to be העלה זאת. Thus <hi type="italic">zoth</hi> will either be closely connected with מי, and make the question sharper and more animated, as is that in <reference osisRef="Gen.12.18">Gen 12:18</reference>, or it will be the subject which then, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Isa 63:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.2">Job 38:2</reference>, cf. below <hi type="italic">Sol 7:5</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.4.11">Jon 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.12">Amo 9:12</reference>, is more closely written with indeterminate participles, according to which it is rightly accented. But we do not translate with Heiligst. <hi type="italic">quid est hoc quod adscendit</hi>, for mī asks after a person, mā after a thing, and only <hi type="italic">per attract</hi>. does mī stand for mā in <reference osisRef="Gen.33.8">Gen 33:8</reference>; Jdg 13:17; Mic 1:5; also not <hi type="italic">quis est hoc</hi> (Vaih.), for <hi type="italic">zoth</hi> after <hi type="italic">mi</hi> has a personal sense, thus: <hi type="italic">quis</hi> (<hi type="italic">quaenam</hi>) <hi type="italic">haec est</hi>. That it is a woman that is being brought forward those who ask know, even if she is yet too far off to be seen by them, because they recognise in the festal gorgeous procession a marriage party. That the company comes up from the wilderness, it may be through the wilderness which separates Jerusalem from Jericho, is in accordance with the fact that a maiden from Galilee is being brought up, and that the procession has taken the way through the Jordan valley (Ghôr); but the scene has also a typical colouring; for the wilderness is, since the time of the Mosaic deliverance out of Egypt, an emblem of the transition from a state of bondage to freedom, from humiliation to glory (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Isa 40:3</reference>; Hos 1:11; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.5">Psa 68:5</reference>). The pomp is like that of a procession before which the censer of frankincense is swung. Columns of smoke from the burning incense mark the line of the procession before and after. תּימרות (תּים) here and at Job 3 (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Norzi) is formed, as it appears, from ימר, to strive upwards, a kindred form to אמר; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">Isa 61:6</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">Isa 17:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.4">Psa 94:4</reference>; the verb תּמר, whence the date-palm receives the name תּמר, is a secondary formation, like תּאב to אבה. Certainly this form תּימרה (cf. on the contrary, תּולדה) is not elsewhere to be supported; Schlottm. sees in it תמּרות, from תּמרה; but such an expansion of the word for <hi type="italic">Dag. dirimens</hi> is scarcely to be supposed. This naming of the pillars of smoke is poet., as <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.3">Jon 3:3</reference>; cf. “a pillar of smoke,” Jdg 20:40. She who approaches comes from the wilderness, brought up to Jerusalem, placed on an elevation, “like pillars of smoke,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, not herself likened thereto, as Schlottm. supposes it must be interpreted (with the <hi type="italic">tertium comp</hi>. of the slender, precious, and lovely), but encompassed and perfumed by such. For her whom the procession brings this lavishing of spices is meant; it is she who is incensed or perfumed with myrrh and frankincense. Schlottm. maintains that מקטּרת cannot mean anything else than “perfumed,” and therefore he reads מקּטרת (as Aq. ἀπὸ θυμιάματος, and Jerome). But the word mekuttěrěth does not certainly stand alone, but with the genit. foll.; and thus as “rent in their clothes,” <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.31">2Sa 13:31</reference>, signifies not such as are themselves rent, but those whose clothes are rent (Ewald, §288 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, compare also de Sacy, II §321), so וגו מקט can also mean those for whom (for whose honour) this incense is expended, and who are thus fumigated with it. מר .t, myrrh, (Arab.) murr (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., above under Sol 1:13), stands also in <reference osisRef="Exod.30.23">Exo 30:23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">Psa 45:9</reference> at the head of the perfumes; it came from Arabia, as did also frankincense levōnā, Arab. lubân (later referred to benzoin); both of the names are Semitic, and the circumstance that the <hi type="italic">Tôra</hi> required myrrh as a component part of the holy oil, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.23">Exo 30:23</reference>, and frankincense as a component part of the holy incense, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.34">Exo 30:34</reference>, points to Arabia as the source whence they were obtained.
