To these two principal spices there is added ממּל (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.6.20">Gen 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.9.2">Gen 9:2</reference>) as an <hi type="italic">et cetera</hi>. רוכל denotes the travelling spice merchants (traders in aromatics), and traders generally. אבקה, which is related to אבק as powder to dust (cf. <hi type="italic">abacus</hi>, a reckoning-table, so named from the sand by means of which arithmetical numbers were reckoned), is the name designating single drugs (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, dry wares; cf. the Arab. elixir = ξηρόν).
entries.79f3b2b056943575d6378706331babfa9b5fca20: Sol 3:7-8 <div eID="gen12559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12560" type="x-p"/> The description of the palanquin now following, one easily attributes to another voice from the midst of the inhabitants of Jerusalem. 7 Lo! Solomon’s palanquin,    Threescore heroes are around it,    Of the heroes of Israel, 8 All of them armed with the sword, expert in war.    Each with his sword on his thigh,    Against fear in the nights. <div eID="gen12560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12561" type="x-p"/> Since אפּריון, 9 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, is not by itself a word clearly intelligible, so as to lead us fully to determine what is here meant by מטּה as distinguished from it, we must let the connection determine. We have before us a figure of that which is called in the post-bibl. Heb. כּלה הכנסת (the bringing-home of the bride). The bridegroom either betook himself to her parents’ house and fetched his bride thence, which appears to be the idea lying at the foundation of Ps 45, if, as we believe, the ivory-palaces are those of the king of Israel’s house; or she was brought to him in festal procession, and he went forth to meet her, 1 Macc. 9:39 - the prevailing custom, on which the parable of the ten virgins (Matt 25) is founded.<note placement="foot">Weigand explains the German word <hi type="italic">Braut</hi> (bride) after the Sanscr. prauḍha, “she who is brought in a carriage;” but this particip. signifies nothing more than (<hi type="italic">aetate</hi>) <hi type="italic">provetca</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen12561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12562" type="x-p"/> Here the bride comes from a great distance; and the difference in rank between the Galilean maid and the king brings this result, that he does not himself go and fetch her, but that she is brought to him. She comes, not as in old times Rebecca did, riding on a camel, but is carried in a mittā, which is surrounded by an escort for protection and as a mark of honour. Her way certainly led through the wilderness, where it was necessary, by a safe convoy, to provide against the possibility (<hi type="italic">min</hi> in mippahad, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Isa 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.4">Isa 25:4</reference>) of being attacked by robbers; whereas it would be more difficult to understand why the marriage-bed in the palace of the king of peace (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.9">1Ch 22:9</reference>) should be surrounded by such an armed band for protection. That Solomon took care to have his chosen one brought to him with royal honours, is seen in the lavish expenditure of spices, the smoke and fragrance of which signalized from afar the approach of the procession, - the mittā, which is now described, can be no other than that in which, sitting or reclining, or half sitting, half reclining, she is placed, who is brought to him in such a cloud of incense. Thus mittā (from nāthā, to stretch oneself out), which elsewhere is also used of a bier, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.21">2Sa 3:21</reference> (like the Talm. ערס = ערשׂ), will here signify a portable bed, a sitting cushion hung round with curtains after the manner of the Indian palanquin, and such as is found on the Turkish caiques or the Venetian gondolas. The appositional nearer definition שׁלּשׁ, “which belonged to Solomon” (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under 6 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), shows that it was a royal palanquin, not one belonging to one of the nobles of the people. The bearers are unnamed persons, regarding whom nothing is said; the sixty heroes form only the guard for safety and for honour (<hi type="italic">sauvegarde</hi>), or the <hi type="italic">escorte</hi> or <hi type="italic">convoie</hi>. The sixty are the tenth part (the <hi type="italic">élite</hi>) of the royal body-guard, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.2">1Sa 27:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.9">1Sa 30:9</reference>, etc. (Schlottm.). If it be asked, Why just 60? we may perhaps not unsuitably reply: The number 60 is here, as at Sol 6:8, the number of Israel multiplied by 5, the fraction of 10; so that thus 60 distinguished warriors form the half to the escort of a king of Israel. חרב אחזי properly means, held fast by the sword so that it goes not let them free, which, according to the sense = holding fast = practised in the use of the sword; the Syr. translation of the Apoc. renders παντοκράτωρ by 'he who is held by all,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, holding it (cf. Ewald, §149 <hi type="italic">b</hi>).<note placement="foot">This deponent use of the <hi type="italic">part. pass</hi>. is common in the Mishna; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Geiger’s <hi type="italic">Lehrbuch zur Sprache der Mishna</hi>, §16. 5.</note>
entries.5901f0394208e3066a8335c45201cd8dfac36c05: Sol 3:9-10 <div eID="gen12562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12563" type="x-p"/> Another voice now describes the splendour of the bed of state which Solomon prepared in honour of Shulamith: 9 A bed of state hath King Solomon made for himself    Of the wood of Lebanon. 10 Its pillars hath he made of silver,      Its support of gold, its cushion of purple;      Its interior is adorned from love      By the daughters of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen12563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12564" type="x-p"/> The sound of the word, the connection and the description, led the Greek translators (the lxx, Venet., and perhaps also others) to render אפּריון, by φορεῖον, litter palanquin (Vulg. <hi type="italic">ferculum</hi>). The <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> here described has a silver pedestal and a purple cushion - as we read in Athenaeus v. 13 (II p. 317, ed. Schweigh.) that the philosopher and tyrant Athenion showed himself “on a silver-legged φορεῖον, with purple coverlet;” and the same author, v. 5 (II p. 253), also says, that on the occasion of a festal procession by Antiochus Epiphanes, behind 200 women who sprinkled ointments from golden urns came 80 women, sitting in pomp on golden-legged, and 500 on silver-legged, φορεῖα - this is the proper name for the costly women's-litter (Suidas: φορεῖον γυναικεῖον), which, according to the number of bearers (Mart. VI 77: six Cappadocians and, ix. 2, eight Syrians), was called ἑξάφορον (<hi type="italic">hexaphorum</hi>, Mart. II 81) or ὀκτώφορον (<hi type="italic">octophorum</hi>, Cicero’s Verr. v. 10). The Mishna, <hi type="italic">Sota</hi> ix. 14, uses <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> in the sense of φορεῖον: “in the last war (that of Hadrian) it was decreed that a bride should not pass through the town in an <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> on account of the danger, but our Rabbis sanctioned it later for modesty’s sake;” as here, “to be carried in an <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi>,” so in Greek, προιέναι (καταστείχειν) ἐν φορείω. In the Midrash also, <hi type="italic">Bamidbar rabba</hi> c. 12, and elsewhere, <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> of this passage before us is taken in all sorts of allegorical significations in most of which the identity of the word with φορεῖον is supposed, which is also there written פּוּרון (after Aruch), cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.49.22">Isa 49:22</reference>, Targ., and is once interchanged with פאפליון, <hi type="italic">papilio</hi> (<hi type="italic">parillon</hi>), pleasure-tent. But a Greek word in the Song is in itself so improbable, that Ewald describes this derivation of the word as a frivolous jest; so much the more improbable, as φορεῖον as the name of a litter (<hi type="italic">lectica</hi>) occurs first in such authors (of the κοινή) as Plutarch, Polybuis, Herodian, and the like, and therefore, with greater right, it may be supposed that it is originally a Semitic word, which the Greek language adopted at the time when the Oriental and Graeco-Roman customs began to be amalgamated. Hence, if mittā <hi type="italic">Sol 3:7</hi>, means a portable bed, -  is evident from this, that it appears as the means of transport with an escort, - then <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> cannot also mean a litter; the description, moreover, does not accord with a litter. We do not read of rings and carrying-poles, but, on the contrary, of pillars (as those of a tent-bed) instead, and, as might be expected, of feet. Schlottm., however, takes mittā and <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> as different names for a portable bed; but the words, “an <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> has King Solomon made,” etc., certainly indicate that he who thus speaks has not the <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> before him, and also that this was something different from the mittā. While Schlottm. is inclined to take <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi>, in the sense of a litter, as a word borrowed from the Greek (but in the time of the first king?), Gesen. in his <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. seeks to derive it, thus understood, from פּרה, <hi type="italic">cito ferri, currere</hi>; but this signification of the verb is imaginary. <div eID="gen12564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12565" type="x-p"/> We expect here, in accordance with the progress of the scene, the name of the bridal couch; and on the supposition that <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi>, <hi type="italic">Sota</hi> 12 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, as in the Mishna, means the litter (Aruch) of the bride, Arab. maziffat, and not <hi type="italic">torus nuptialis</hi> (Buxt.), then there is a possibility that <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> is a more dignified word for 'ěrěs, Sol 1:17, yet sufficient thereby to show that פּוּריא is the usual Talm. name of the marriage-bed (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Mezia</hi> 23 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, where it stand, <hi type="italic">per meton</hi>., for <hi type="italic">concubitus</hi>), which is wittily explained by שׁפרין ורבין עליה (<hi type="italic">Kethuboth</hi> 10 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, and elsewhere). The Targ. has for it the form פּוּרין (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Levy). It thus designates a bed with a canopy (a tent-bed), <reference osisRef="Deut.32.50">Deu 32:50</reference>, Jerus; so that the ideas of the bed of state and the palanquin (cf. כילה, canopy, and כילת חתנים, bridal-bed, <hi type="italic">Succa</hi> 11 <hi type="italic">a</hi>) touch one another. In general, פוריא (פורין, as is also the case with <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi>, must have been originally a common designation of certain household furniture with a common characteristic; for the Syr. aprautha, plur. parjevatha (Wiseman’s <hi type="italic">Horae</hi>, p. 255), or also parha (Castell.), signifies a cradle. It is then to be inquired, whether this word is referable to a root-word which gives a common characteristic with manifold applications. But the Heb. פּרה, from the R. pr, signifies to split,<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Friedr. Delitzsch’s <hi type="italic">Indogerman.-semit. Studien</hi>, p. 72.</note> to tear asunder, to break forth, to bring fruit, to be fruitful, and nothing further. Paaraa has nowhere the signification to run, as already remarked; only in the Palest.-Aram. פּרא is found in this meaning (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Buxt.). The Arab. farr does not signify to run, but to flee; properly (like our “<hi type="italic">ausreissen</hi>” = be tear out, to break out), to break open by flight the rank in which one stands (as otherwise turned by horse-dealers: to open wide the horse’s mouth). But, moreover, we do not thus reach the common characteristic which we are in search of; for if we may say of the litter that it runs, yet we cannot say that of a bed or a cradle, etc. The Arab. farfâr, <hi type="italic">species vehiculi muliebris</hi>, also does not help us; for the verb farfar, to vacillate, to shake, is its appropriate root-word.<note placement="foot">The Turkish Kâmûs says of farfâr: “it is the name of a vehicle (merkeb), like the camel-litter (haudej), destined merely for women.” This also derives its name from rocking to and fro. So farfâr, for farfara is to the present day the usual word for <hi type="italic">agiter, sécouer les ailes</hi>; farfarah, for <hi type="italic">légèreté</hi>; furfûr, for butterfly (cf. Ital. farfalla); generally, the ideas of that which is light and of no value - <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, a babbler-connect themselves with the root far in several derivatives.</note> <div eID="gen12565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12566" type="x-p"/> With better results shall we compare the Arab. fary, which, in <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>., signifies to break open, to cut out (<hi type="italic">couper, tailler une étoffe</hi>), and also, figuratively, to bring forth something strange, something not yet existing (yafry alfaryya, according to the Arab. <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>. = yaty bal'ajab fy 'amalh, he accomplishes something wonderful); the primary meaning in <hi type="italic">Conj</hi>. viii. is evidently: yftarra kidban, to cut out lies, to meditate and to express that which is calumnious (a similar metaphor to khar'a, <hi type="italic">findere</hi>, viii. <hi type="italic">fingere</hi>, to cut out something in the imagination; French, <hi type="italic">inventer</hi>, <hi type="italic">imaginer</hi>). With this fary, however, we do not immediately reach פּוּריא, אפּריון; for fary, as well as fara (farw), are used only of cutting to pieces, cutting out, sewing together of leather and other materials (cf. Arab. farwat, fur; farrā, furrier), but not of cutting and preparing wood. <div eID="gen12566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12567" type="x-p"/> But why should not the Semitic language have used פּרה, פּרא, also, in the sense of the verb בּרא, which signifies<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Friedr. Delitzsch’s <hi type="italic">Indogerm.-sem. Stud</hi>. p. 50. We are now taught by the Assyr. that as בן goes back to בנה, so בר (Assyr. nibru) to ברה = ברא, to bring forth.</note> to cut and hew, in the sense of forming (cf. <hi type="italic">Pih</hi>. כּרא, <hi type="italic">sculpere</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.24">Eze 21:24</reference>), as in the Arab. bara and bary, according to Lane, mean, “be formed or fashioned by cutting (a writing-reed, stick, bow), shaped out, or pared,” - in other words: Why should פרה, used in the Arab. of the cutting of leather, not be used, in the Heb. and Aram., of the preparing of wood, and thus of the fashioning of a bed or carriage? As חשּׁבון signifies a machine, and that the work of an engineer, so פּריון signifies timber-work, carpenter-work, and, lengthened especially by <hi type="italic">Aleph prosthet</hi>., a product of the carpenter’s art, a bed of state. The <hi type="italic">Aleph prosth</hi>. would indeed favour the supposition that <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> is a foreign word; for the Semitic language frequently forms words after this manner, - <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, אמגּוּשׁא, a magician; אסמּרא, a stater.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Merx’s <hi type="italic">Gramm. Syr</hi>. p. 115.</note> <div eID="gen12567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12568" type="x-p"/> But apart from such words as אגרטל, oddly sounding in accord with κάρταλλος as <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> with φορεῖον, אבטּיח and אבעבּעה are examples of genuine Heb. words with such a prosthesis, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, an <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi>, as in אכזב and the like. אפּדן, palace, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.45">Dan 11:45</reference>, is, for its closer amalgamation by means of <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>., at least an analogous example; for thus it stands related to the Syr. opadna, as, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, (Syr.), oparsons, net, Ewald, §163 <hi type="italic">c</hi>, to the Jewish-Aram. אפרסנא, or אפּרסנא; cf. also אפּתם, “finally,” in relation to the Pehlv. אפדוּם (Spiegel’s <hi type="italic">Literatur der Parsen</hi>, p. 356).<note placement="foot">אּפוּריא, quoted by Gesen. in his <hi type="italic">Thes., Sanhedrin</hi> 109 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, is not applicable here, it is contracted from אד־פוריא (on the bed).</note> <div eID="gen12568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12569" type="x-p"/> We think we have thus proved that אפּריון is a Heb. word, which, coming from the verb פּרה, to cut right, to make, frame, signifies<note placement="foot">This derivation explains how it comes that <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> can mean, in the Karaite Heb., a bird-cage or aviary, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Gottlober’s ס בקרת, p. 208. We have left out of view the phrase אפריון נמטיי ליה, which, in common use, means: we present to him homage (of approbation or thanks). It occurs first, as uttered by the Sassanidean king, Shabur I, <hi type="italic">Mezia</hi> 119 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, <hi type="italic">extr.</hi>; and already Rapoport, in his <hi type="italic">Erech Millîn</hi>, 1852, p. 183, has recognised this word <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> as Pers. It is the Old Pers. âfrîna or âfrivana (from frî, to love), which signifies blessing or benediction (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Justi’s <hi type="italic">Handb. d. Zendsprache</hi>, p. 51). Rashi is right in glossing it by חן שׁלנו (the testimony of our favour).</note> a bed, and that, as Ewald also renders, a bed of state. רפידה (from רפד, R. רף, to lift from beneath, <hi type="italic">sublevare</hi>, then <hi type="italic">sternere</hi>) is the head of the head of the bed; lxx ἀνάκλιτον; Jerome, <hi type="italic">reclinatorium</hi>, which, according to Isidore, is the Lat. vulgar name for the <hi type="italic">fulchra</hi>, the reclining (of the head and foot) of the bedstead. Schlottmann here involuntarily bears testimony that <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> may at least be understood of a bed of state as well as of a litter of state; for he remarks: “The four sides of the bed were generally adorned with carved work, ivory, metal, or also, as in the case of most of the Oriental divans, with drapery.” “<hi type="italic">Nec mihi tunc</hi>,” says Porpertius, ii. 10, 11, “<hi type="italic">fulcro lectus sternatur eburno</hi>.” Here the <hi type="italic">fulcrum</hi> is not of ivory, but of gold. מרכּב (from רכב, to lie upon anything; Arab. II componere; Aethiop. adipisci) is that which one takes possession of, sitting or lying upon it, the cushion, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, of a saddle (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.9">Lev 15:9</reference>); here, the divan (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Lane, <hi type="italic">Mod. Egypt</hi>, I 10) arranged on an elevated frame, serving both as a seat and as a couch. Red purple is called ארגּמן, probably from רגם = רקם, as material of variegated colour. By the interior תּוך of the bed, is probably meant a covering which lay above this cushion. רצף, to arrange together, to combine (whence רצפה, pavement; Arab. ruṣafat, a paved way), is here meant like στορέννυμι, στόρνυμι, στρώννυμι, whence στρῶμα. And רצוּף אה is not equivalent to רצוּף אה (after the construction 1Ki 22:10; <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">Eze 9:2</reference>), inlaid with love, but is the adv. accus of the manner; “love” (cf. hhesed, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Psa 141:5</reference>) denotes the motive: laid out or made up as a bed from love on the part of the daughters of Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the ladies of the palace - these from love to the king have procured a costly tapestry or tapestries, which they have spread over the purple cuchion. Thus rightly Vaihinger in his <hi type="italic">Comm</hi>., and Merx, <hi type="italic">Archiv</hi>. Bd. II 111-114. Schlottmann finds this interpretation of מן “stiff and hard;” but although מן in the pass. is not used like the Greek ὑπό, yet it can be used like ἀπό (Ewald, sec. 295 <hi type="italic">b</hi>); and if there be no actual example of this, yet we point to Ps 45 in illustration of the custom of presenting gifts to a newly-married pair. He himself understands אהבה personally, as do also Ewald, Heiligst., Böttcher; “the voice of the people,” says Ewald, “knows that the finest ornament with which the invisible interior of the couch is adorned, is a love from among the daughters of Jerusalem, - <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, some one of the court ladies who was raised, from the king’s peculiar love to her, to the rank of a queen-consort. The speaker thus ingeniously names this newest favourite 'a love,' and at the same time designates her as the only thing with which this elegant structure, all adorned on the outside is adorned within.” Relatively better Böttcher: with a love (beloved one), <hi type="italic">prae filiis Hierus</hi>. But even though אהבה, like amor and amores, might be used of the beloved one herself, yet רצוף does not harmonize with this, seeing we cannot speak of being paved or tapestried with persons. Schlottm. in vain refers for the personal signification of אהבה to Sol 2:7, where it means love and nothing else, and seeks to bring it into accord with רצוף; for he remarks, “as the stone in mosaic work fills the place destined for it, so the bride the interior of the litter, which is intended for just one person filling it.” But is this not more comical, without intending to be so, than Juvenal’s (i. 1. 32 s.):<hi type="italic">Causidici nova cum veniat lectica Mathonis Plena ipso</hi> ... . <div eID="gen12569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12570" type="x-p"/> But Schlottm. agrees with us in this, that the marriage which is here being prepared for was the consummation of the happiness of Solomon and Shulamith, not of another woman, and not the consummation of Solomon’s assault on the fidelity of Shulamith, who hates him to whom she now must belong, loving only one, the shepherd for whom she is said to sigh (<hi type="italic">Sol 1:4</hi>), that he would come and take her away. “This triumphal procession,” says Rocke,<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Das Hohelied, Erstlingsdrama, u.s.w.</hi> The Song, a Primitive Drama from the East; or, Family Sins and Love’s Devotion. A Moral Mirror for the Betrothed and Married, 1851.</note> “was for her a mourning procession, the royal litter a bier; her heart died within her with longing for her beloved shepherd.” Touching, if it were only true! Nowhere do we see her up to this point resisting; much rather she is happy in her love. The shepherd-hypothesis cannot comprehend this marriage procession without introducing incongruous and imaginary things; it is a poem of the time of Gellert. Solomon the seducer, and Shulamith the heroine of virtue, are figures as from Gellert’s Swedish Countess; they are moral commonplaces personified, but not real human beings. In the litter sits Shulamith, and the <hi type="italic">appiryon</hi> waits for her. Solomon rejoices that now the reciprocal love-bond is to find its conclusion; and what Shulamith, who is brought from a lowly to so lofty a station, experiences, we shall hear her describe in the sequel.
entries.dfa1604921a3371e1df9e87c292e1a7d29eefc3e: Sol 3:11 <div eID="gen12570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12571" type="x-p"/> At the close of the scene, the call now goes forth to the daughters of Zion, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the women of Jerusalem collectively, to behold the king, who now shows himself to the object of his love and to the jubilant crowd, as the festal procession approaches. 11 Come out, yet daughters of Zion, and see      King Solomon with the crown      With which his mother crowned him      On the day of his espousal,      And on the day of the gladness of his heart. <div eID="gen12571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12572" type="x-p"/> The women of the court, as distinguished from the Galilean maiden, are called “daughters of Jerusalem;” here, generally, the women of Zion or Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.11">Lam 5:11</reference>) are called “daughters of Zion.” Instead of צאנה (since the verb <hi type="italic">Lamed Aleph</hi> is treated after the manner of verbs <hi type="italic">Lamed He</hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.50.20">Jer 50:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.49">Eze 23:49</reference>), צאינה, and that defect. צאנה,<note placement="foot">Without the <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> after <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi> in the older ed. Thus also in J and H with the note לית וחסר [= <hi type="italic">nonnisi h. l. et defective</hi>] agreeing with the MS Masora Parna. Thus also Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 108 <hi type="italic">b</hi>.</note> is used for the sake of assonance with וּראינה;<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">Resh</hi> has in H <hi type="italic">Chatef-Pathach</hi>, with <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> preceding. This, according to Ben-Asher’s rule, is correct (cf. Psa 28:9. וּר). In the punctuation of the <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi> with <hi type="italic">Tsere</hi> or <hi type="italic">Segol</hi> the Codd. vary, according to the different views of the punctuation. J has <hi type="italic">Segol</hi>; D H, <hi type="italic">Tsere</hi>, which latter also Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 109 <hi type="italic">a</hi>.</note> elsewhere also, as we have shown at <reference osisRef="Isa.22.13">Isa 22:13</reference>, an unusual form is used for the sake of the sound. It is seen from the <hi type="italic">Sota</hi> (ix. 14) that the old custom for the bridegroom to wear a “crown” was abolished in consequence of the awful war with Vespasian. Rightly Epstein, against Grätz, shows from <reference osisRef="Job.31.36">Job 31:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.4">Psa 103:4</reference>, that men also crowned themselves. בּעטרה (with the crown) is, according to the best authorities, without the art., and does not require it, since it is determined by the relat. clause following. חתנה is the marriage (the word also used in the post-bibl. Heb., and interchanging with חפּה, properly νυμφών, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.15">Mat 9:15</reference>), from the verb חתן, which, proceeding from the root-idea of cutting into (Arab. khatn, to circumcise; R. חת .R ;, whence חתך, חתם, חתר), denotes the pressing into, or going into, another family; חתן is he who enters into such a relation of affinity, and חטן the father of her who is taken away, who also on his part is related to the husband.<note placement="foot">L. Geiger (<hi type="italic">Ursprung der Sprache</hi>, 1869, p. 88) erroneously finds in R. חת (חתם, etc.) the meaning of binding. The (Arab.) noun Khatan means first a married man, and then any relation on the side of the wife (Lane); the fundamental idea must be the same as that of Khatn, circumcidere (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.4.25">Exo 4:25</reference>), viz., that of penetrating, which חתת, <hi type="italic">percellere</hi>, and נחת, <hi type="italic">descendere</hi> (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">ferrum descendit haud alte in corpus</hi>, in Livy, and <reference osisRef="Prov.17.1">Pro 17:1</reference>), also exhibit.</note> <div eID="gen12572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12573" type="x-p"/> Here also the seduction fable is shattered. The marriage with Shulamith takes place with the joyful consent of the queen-mother. In order to set aside this fatal circumstance, the “crown” is referred back to the time when Solomon was married to Pharaoh’s daughter. <hi type="italic">Cogitandus est Salomo, says Heiligst., qui cum Sulamitha pompa sollemni Hierosolyma redit, eadem corona nuptiali ornatus, qua quum filiam regis Aegyptiorum uxorem duxeret ornatus erat</hi>. But was he then so poor or niggardly as to require to bring forth this old crown? and so basely regardless of his legitimate wife, of equal rank with himself, as to wound her by placing this crown on his head in honour of a rival? No; at the time when this youthful love-history occurred, Pharaoh’s daughter was not yet married. The mention of his mother points us to the commencement of his reign. His head is not adorned with a crown which had already been worn, but with a fresh garland which his mother wreathed around the head of her youthful son. The men have already welcomed the procession from afar; but the king in his wedding attire has special attractions for the women - they are here called upon to observe the moment when the happy pair welcome one another.  <chapter eID="Song.3"/> <div eID="gen12573" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. III.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 BY night on my bed <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either 1. In a time of Tribulation. which is commonly sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nified by the <ns0:hi>Night,</ns0:hi> and somtimes by a <ns0:hi>Bed,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Revel.</ns0:hi> 2. 22, Or 2. When I expected to find him; for the Husband who by his occa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sions is oft forced to be absent from his Wife in the day time, but at night returns to her, and beds with her. Or 3. When others compose themselves to rest and sleep, my Thoughts were troubled, and my Affections were working towards him, and I was very de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sirous to enjoy him.</ns0:note> I sought him <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">I sought for Christs gracious and powerful Presence, in, and by, the Word, and Prayer, and Meditation.</ns0:note> whom my soul loveth: I sought him <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This repetition notes her perseverance and unweariedness in seeking him.</ns0:note>, but I found him not <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">For he had withdrawn himself, and the mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />festations of his Love from me, either because I had not sought him diligently, or because I had abused his favour, or to try and exercise my Faith, and Patience, and Love, and other Graces.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 I will rise now <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">I will immediately apply my self to seek him, without whom my bed can give me no rest nor comfort.</ns0:note>, and go about the city <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The City of God, the Church in which Christ resides.</ns0:note> in the streets, and in the broad ways <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Not finding him in private Prayer, and Meditation, I sought him in the places of publick Assemblies, and Ordinances; for the People frequently met to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gether in the streets, not only for civil, but for religious ends, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 32. 6. <ns0:hi>Neh.</ns0:hi> 8. 1, 3, 16. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 1. 20. 21. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 13. 26.</ns0:note>, I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He saw fit still to delay the discoveries of his Grace, partly to chastise my former folly, partly to try my sincerity and constancy, and partly that he might be more welcome when he came to me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 5. 7.</ns0:note> The watch-men <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Ministers of Christ, and Rulers of the Church, who are oft called <ns0:hi>Watchmen,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 62. 6. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 3. 17. and elsewhere.</ns0:note> that go about the city <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To prevent disorders and dangers by night.</ns0:note>, found me <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Whilest they walked round about the City, according to their duty.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>to whom I said</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Without ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther fear or shame, as being transported and wholly swallowed up with Love.</ns0:note>, Saw ye <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> whom my soul loveth <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">She doth not name him, because she thought it needless, as supposing that a Person of such transcendent excellen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy could not be unknown to men in that publick capacity. Their answer is not mentioned, either because they gave her no answer, at least no satisfactory answer, or because by their silence she ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thered that they were unable, or unwilling to inform her; and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing eager in the pursuit of her beloved, she would not lose time in impertinent discourses with them.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:hi>It was</ns0:hi> but a little that I passed from them, but I found him <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Christ met me, and manifested his Love to me, according to his Promise made to those that seek him constantly and diligently, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 8. 17. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 7. 7. &c.</ns0:note> whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Being taught by my late experi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence how doleful a thing it was to lose him, and how hard it was to find and recover him when he was lost.</ns0:note>, until I had brought him into my mothers house <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That there I might entertain and embrace him, and gain my Mothers consent, and so proceed to the consummation of the Marriage. She saith her <ns0:hi>Mothers,</ns0:hi> rather than her <ns0:hi>Fathers,</ns0:hi> House, because the Men and the Women had several and separated apartments in the House. For the mystical meaning which is the principal sense intended in this Book, as the Spouse here, and in many other places in this Book, signifies particular Believers, so her Mother is the univer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sal Church, or the true <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> which hath its rise from <ns0:hi>above, which is the Mother of us all,</ns0:hi> Gal. 4. 26. in which Christ and Belie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers are united, and have sweet communion together in holy Or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinances, into which Believers are said to bring Christ by Faith, and Prayer, and the preparation of their Hearts for him, whereby they invite and in some sort ingage Christ to go with them into the publick Assemblies, and there to give them his Loves, although otherwise it is Christ who properly brings Believers into the Church. But all particulars in Allegorical Scriptures, are not to be strictly urged, as all learned Interpreters agree, many being added only for the decency of the Allegory.</ns0:note>, and into the chamber of her that conceived me <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Christ is as it were the Father that begets, and the Church the Mother that con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceiveth and bringeth forth Believers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 2. 7. & 8. 4.</ns0:note> I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> love till he please <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This verse is repeated from <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 2. 7. where it is explained. The Spouse exhorts her self, and all her fellow-Members to be ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry circumspect, lest by any unkind or provoking carriage, they should give Christ any cause to depart from them. He is suppo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed to allude to the custom of awakening the Bridegroom and Bride by Songs and musical instruments.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 8. 5.</ns0:note> Who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The persons speaking seem to be the Daughters of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> who upon occasion of the Brides Speech to them, make this reply, or the Friends of the Bridegroom: The person spoken of is the Spouse or Bride.</ns0:note> that cometh out of the wilderness <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">From the Country, which in comparison of Cities, is oft called a <ns0:hi>Wilderness,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 42. 11. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 1. 80. & 3. 2. and elsewhere, from whence we little expected to see so beautiful and glorious a Bride to come, such Persons being usually bred in Courts or noble Cities. This Phrase implies that Believers were and were to be called out of the World, which for its barrennes<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, and disorder, and replenishment with wild Beasts, may fitly be compared to a Wilderness, and not only out of the Holy Land, which was as the Garden of God, but also out of the Gentile-World, which in Prophetical Writings is frequently described un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the notion of a <ns0:hi>Wilderness,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 35. 1. & 43. 19, 20. Withal he seems to allude to the People of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> which to the wonder and astonishment of all those parts came up out of the Wilderness into <ns0:hi>Canaan.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> like pillars of smoak <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">To which the Church may not unfitly be compa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red, partly for its excellent order and comely proportions, partly for its direct and constant motion towards Heaven, and partly to imply that though she was really and inwardly glorious, yet she was outwardly obscure and despicable in the eyes of the World. Possibly the words may be rendred thus, <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> with (which particle is very frequently understood, as hath been shewed in divers forego<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Texts) <ns0:hi>Pillars</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>a Pillar</ns0:hi> (for the plural number is oft put for the singular) <ns0:hi>of smoak.</ns0:hi> And so the sense may be either 1. Being conducted out of the Wilderness as by a Pillar of smoak going be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore them, as the Israelites were led through the Wilderness to <ns0:hi>Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />naan,</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>a Pillar of Cloud and Fire,</ns0:hi> Exod. 13. 21, 22. Or rather 2. Attended with many Prayers and Praises, and other holy per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formances, which are perpetually ascending from her, and offered by her unto God. So he alludes to those Pillars of smoak which all the day long ascended from those numerous Sacrifices which were offered in the Temple, which also was a Type of the Prayers of the Saints offered by Christ unto his Father, as may be gathered from <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 8. 3, 4, 5. But this I only propose.</ns0:note>, perfumed <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">This doth not belong to the <ns0:hi>Pillars,</ns0:hi> as appears by the difference of the numbers in the Hebrew words, <ns0:hi>the Pillars</ns0:hi> being plural, and this word singular, but to the Person, to wit, the Spouse, who is said to be thus perfumed; partly for her good Name or Renown, which is compared to per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fumes, <ns0:hi>Eccl.</ns0:hi> 7. 1. partly for her excellent Virtues and religious Services which are pleasant and acceptable to God, and to Angels, and Men; and partly for the Merits and Graces of Christ, which are a <ns0:hi>sweet savour</ns0:hi> to God, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 5. 2. and wherewith she is enriched and beautified.</ns0:note> with myrrhe and frankincense, with all powders of the merchant <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Which are setched by the Merchants from <ns0:hi>Ara<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bia,</ns0:hi> or other remote parts of the World for the use of perfuming.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Behold, his bed <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">These are the words either 1. Of the Bridemen, who spake <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. and here continue their speech, and from the admiration of the Bride proceed to the admiration of the Bridegroom. Or 2. Of the Spouse, who being admired by the Bridemen, turns their Eyes and Thoughts to the Bridegroom, and directs them to the study of his excellencies, and intimates that all her comfort and safety is from him. The <ns0:hi>Bed,</ns0:hi> the place of rest and conjugal converse, seems to denote the Church, which is comely through Christs Beauty, and safe by his Protection, in which Christ is glorified, and Believers enjoy sweet fellowship with him, both here in the Church militant, and especially hereafter in the Church trium<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phant.</ns0:note>, which <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Solomons <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which is the Bed, not of an ordinary Man, but of a great King, whom <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> represents or typifies, and who is greater than <ns0:hi>Solomon.</ns0:hi> Nor is it hard to understand the <ns0:hi>Messias</ns0:hi> under the name of <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> his Type and Progenitor, seeing he is, upon the same reason, called <ns0:hi>David, Ier.</ns0:hi> 30. 9. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 34. 23. and elsewhere, especially considering that this whole Book is by the confession both of Jewish and Christian Interpreters to be mystically under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood.</ns0:note>, three<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />score <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> very many, the certain number being put for an uncertain, as is frequent.</ns0:note> valiant men <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> about it, of the valiant of Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He alludes to <ns0:hi>Solomons</ns0:hi> Guard, or Watchmen, whereby he designs all those Creatures, whether An<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gels, Princes, Ministers, or others, whose Ministry God useth for the Protection of his Church.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 They all hold swords, being expert in war: every man <ns0:hi>hath</ns0:hi> his sword upon his thigh <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Is prepared and ready to fight, as this Phrase notes, <ns0:hi>Ex.</ns0:hi> 32 27. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 45. 3.</ns0:note>, because of fear in the night <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To prevent those dangers and mischiefs which are most frequent, and most dreadful in the night season. <ns0:hi>The night</ns0:hi> may note either 1. The whole time of this Life, which may well be called <ns0:hi>night</ns0:hi> in respect of that ignorance and Errour, and other kinds of Darkness wherewith it is attended, as the future Life is compared to a <ns0:hi>day,</ns0:hi> this Life being the only time wherein such a Guard is necessary.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
